data.title: 50% are losing money; computing centers are largely gathering dust.
data.description:
Nearly 900 million yuan in computing power services were sold in half a year, with net profit increasing sevenfold.

This is Parallel Technology's "harvest" in the first half of 2026. Similarly, several AI giants also have "almost no idle GPUs."

On the other hand, a thousand-GPU-level intelligent computing center in a western city has an occupancy rate of less than 50%, and the actual utilization rate of the servers already on the platform is less than 30%, yet its annual operating costs exceed 30 million yuan. Industry insiders estimate that the utilization rate of intelligent computing centers nationwide is only about 20%-30%.

While scrambling for GPUs, they are running idle.

The high-performance, large-scale, and stable clusters needed by leading AI companies remain scarce; some regions have built computing power in advance, but have not found matching customers and applications.

Lingkong Intelligent founder Peng Yuanyang told LeadDao that many companies don't lack the desire to use AI, but rather don't know which models to use, how much computing power to buy, how to process the data, how to deploy the system, or whether this investment will ultimately bring revenue or cost reduction. There's a missing layer of "connection" between computing power and enterprise needs. - 01 – Who Makes Money First? Peng Yuanyang observed that some small computing power leasing companies in Shenzhen are actually doing quite well. They don't have massive clusters, but they're willing to take on small orders of a few or dozens of cards, getting closer to their customers and understanding better what models their customers are running and how long they need them. Parallel Technology, on the other hand, has taken this business to a much larger scale. In the first half of 2026, the company's computing power service revenue reached 895 million yuan, accounting for 94.62% of total revenue; enterprise customer computing power service revenue reached 705 million yuan, a year-on-year increase of 168.07%. Its core is not simply selling cards from a single data center, but rather integrating computing power resources from different regions and clusters through a computing network, and then scheduling and delivering them. This is a business that improves turnover rate. The recently launched "Computing Power Supermarket" in Jiangning, Nanjing provides another example. During the trial operation phase, only 20 companies connected, but the model was called 1.308 million times, consuming 51 billion tokens. China Electric Transformer Co., Ltd. previously wanted to use a large model for bidding document review and code review, but the team was consistently hampered by computing power pricing and model selection. After connecting to the "computing power supermarket," enterprises can directly select GPUs and mainstream large-scale models for on-demand use. Enterprises do have AI needs, but their past methods of purchasing computing power were too cumbersome. Previously, a short-term project might require renting an entire server and signing a long-term contract; now, more and more platforms charge by card time, core time, or even tokens. Enterprises only pay for actual use, while computing power companies can break down a batch of GPUs into more orders. This is what "computing power supermarkets," "computing power banks," GPU leasing, and computing power scheduling platforms are all doing: repackaging scattered, heterogeneous, and idle computing power into purchasable standard services. However, this matching process isn't extremely profitable. Parallel Technology's gross profit margin for computing power services in the first half of the year was 16.97%. This means that simply selling cards from A to B doesn't yield the profit margin one might imagine. What truly determines profits is whether the same batch of GPUs can be used by more customers for a longer period of time. - 02 – While scrambling for GPUs, many are idle. Why are so many intelligent computing centers "sleeping" despite such high computing power demand? Many places build intelligent computing centers following the infrastructure logic: first determine the scale, buy equipment, build the center, and then wait for demand to come in. But computing power isn't like a highway; once it's built, cars won't automatically come. A survey by Xinhua News Agency's *Banyue Tan* magazine found that a province in central China plans three intelligent computing centers with a total capacity of 1200 PFLOPS (petaflops), but the local digital economy enterprises number less than 100, and the actual demand is less than 200 PFLOPS. In an eastern city, two districts and counties are building intelligent computing centers for biomedicine and industrial internet respectively, but fewer than 10 enterprises have actually moved in. According to data released by the National Bureau of Data Science, as of June 2026, China had over 500 intelligent computing centers in operation, with nearly 400 more under construction or planned. If the industry average utilization rate of these 500 intelligent computing centers is only 20%-30%, and a single intelligent computing center typically needs to reach around 40% utilization to break even, then roughly 250-350 centers may still be operating at a loss or struggling to cover their full costs. Large-scale model training requires high-performance chips, high-speed interconnects, storage, cluster stability, and a mature software ecosystem; industrial and financial scenarios may have different requirements regarding latency, data security, and privatization. Having idle GPUs in a location doesn't mean it can directly handle the training tasks of leading model companies. This is why "giants lacking computing power" and "local computing power being idle" occur simultaneously. Many ordinary enterprises don't know how to find suitable computing power. A factory might only want to do visual quality inspection, a retail company might only want to integrate customer service, and a company might only need a private knowledge base. The project scale might only involve a few or dozens of GPUs, yet people still need to handle model selection, data, deployment, security, and cost. Peng Yuanyang said there's a lot of "dirty work" involved. Large companies prefer to build standardized platforms, making it difficult to enter fragmented scenarios one by one; smaller companies are willing to do so, but their service chains are not yet mature. What computing centers often lack is not the next batch of GPUs, but the next batch of orders. - 03 – What's truly valuable is the Token. Peng Yuanyang believes that for most ordinary enterprises, what they are buying in the long term is inference computing power, which means directly calling existing models and integrating AI into customer service, marketing, code development, industrial inspection, and knowledge bases. Training has a project cycle, but inference occurs continuously along with the business. This is changing the financial model of computing power companies. Qingyun Technology's AI computing power cloud service revenue in 2025 was 43.36 million yuan, a year-on-year decrease, but its gross profit margin increased from 18.99% to 31.62%. One of the reasons the company cited was improved utilization of computing resources and optimized operating costs. Another company showcased another side of the asset-heavy business. Runjian Technology's computing power network business revenue in the first half of 2026 was 519 million yuan, a year-on-year increase of 50.31%, and it claimed that its "Token Factory" business model was basically closed-loop; however, the gross profit margin of this business was only 6.97%. The company explained that one of the main reasons was the high depreciation in the early stages of fixed asset investment. Both sets of figures point to the same fact: buying GPUs is just the beginning. Depreciation still occurs as long as the cards are idle; once utilization increases, each additional task run can potentially reduce fixed costs. Therefore, the next wave of opportunities may not belong to those who build another intelligent computing center, but rather to those who can generate more tokens from the same batch of cards. GPU scheduling, elastic inference, inference acceleration, multi-model routing, and cost optimization represent the first layer of opportunities; further down are model deployment, privatization, enterprise knowledge bases, agents, and vertical industry applications. The latter are closer to the customer's money. When AI remains in the demo stage, computing power consumption is a one-time event; once it enters the production stage, with factories conducting daily quality inspections, customer service handling daily orders, and programmers writing code daily, computing power becomes a continuous source of revenue. Peng Yuanyang believes that the most important thing for intelligent computing centers is to provide stable and low-cost infrastructure, rather than handling all applications themselves. Companies that truly understand the industry should then integrate models and computing power into enterprise business. More than 500 intelligent computing centers nationwide have already been built there. In the next phase, the industry competition won't just be about "who has more GPUs." More importantly, it will be about who can minimize the downtime of a GPU and generate one more collectible token; and who can turn these tokens into a service that businesses are willing to renew for long-term subscriptions.

data.title: Everything can be paired: A comprehensive guide to Robinhood's new on-chain platform, CME.
data.description:
Author: Gemini, Deep Tide TechFlow

A few days ago, the entire internet was discussing the liquidity diversion caused by the decline in Robinhood Chain's 24-hour DEX trading volume from $3 billion. Today, it seems that the one-day on-chain bear market has ended.

Some leading companies on the RH chain, such as Pons and Cashcat, have seen a certain degree of rebound. At the same time, on-chain speculative capital has not truly left the market; they are simply looking for the next narrative maker.

If the past two weeks saw platforms represented by Pons and Long pushing the "coin-stock pairing" model of "pricing memes with Nvidia and Tesla tokens" to its climax;

then today, funds on the RH chain are beginning to experience aesthetic fatigue with homogeneous stock-like tokens.

Instead, a new launchpad, the Commodity Market Exchange, emerged; its token, CME, saw its market capitalization surpass $15 million, with daily trading volume approaching $10 million. So what exactly is everyone rushing for? The answer is that it pioneered a completely new token issuance method, extremely abstract yet distinct from traditional token-stock pairings: token-merchant (product) pairings, or what could be called "everything can be paired." If you thought the previous round of "token-stock pairings" using Nvidia and Tesla to price Meme was novel enough, then CME has taken this approach to another level. Can all commodities be MEME-denominated assets? Crypto has never disappointed when it comes to creating entertaining content. In traditional DEXs, MEME asset trading pairs are generally stablecoins, ETH, or on-chain stocks in the current crypto-stock market. Now, the pool assets for this platform have been expanded to include 94 real-world commodities and non-standard assets. For example, using a fart coin ($FART) with natural gas as the pool base, paired with on-chain milk prices ($MILKERS); and agricultural tokens paired with crude oil and corn. Furthermore, you can even create pools with non-standard consumer goods, pairing MEMEs with McDonald's Big Mac, CS2 Dragon Lore skins, Pokémon's first-generation Charizard cards, and so on. This free-play approach has allowed meme speculators to come up with all sorts of creative ideas. Buying $WEN, with the underlying pool being a "Lamborghini," is essentially a self-deprecating joke: when (when) will I be able to buy a Lamborghini? There's no real gold or silver involved, only a one-sided pool and oracles. Many newcomers often have the misconception: "Does buying a gold-paired meme indirectly mean holding real gold?" The answer is clearly no. Unlike Robinhood's official compliant brokerage system, which features tokenized US stocks (Stock Tokens) or precious metal ETFs, the commodities on the CME platform do not actually achieve off-chain physical delivery or warehouse receipt custody. To enable Meme to pool with real-world assets, the platform has built its own lightweight synthetic asset system: It issues 94 ERC-20 commodity tokens: the platform itself has minted tokens such as Gold Coin, Crude Oil Coin, and Milk Coin, each token representing a corresponding unit of commodity price (e.g., 1 bushel of corn or 1 ounce of gold). The protocol then captures real-time reference prices from near-month commodity futures prices, fast food menu prices, and TCGplayer card order books, with an update cycle of approximately 60 seconds. A one-way Uniswap pool is established between the commodity coin and the stablecoin USDG. Protocol sell orders are placed one level above the reference price, and buy orders are placed one level below the reference price. When the real-world price changes or the liquidity on one side is exhausted, the off-chain Keeper bot quickly cancels the orders and migrates the pool to the latest price. In short, players are not actually interacting with physical assets, but with a set of "commodity-synthetic stablecoins" whose price exposure is maintained by algorithms and oracles. Essentially, the concept of synthetic assets is not new, but thanks to the hype surrounding coin-stock pairings and the idea that everything can be paired, this has attracted the interest of on-chain developers. Aggressive Allocation Model Attracts Funds to Buy Tokens Any on-chain micro-innovation, without the expectation of wealth creation and a biased distribution of benefits, will find it difficult to attract liquidity on the first day. CME was able to drive its platform token $CME's market capitalization to the $15 million range in a short period of time, primarily due to its aggressive adjustments to its business model and token economics: 40% of transaction fees are automatically distributed as dividends: 40% of the platform's transaction fees are directly and automatically distributed to token holders in the form of "corresponding commodity tokens" according to their holding weight, with a settlement every 15 minutes and no manual claim required. Buying milk (meme tokens) will result in "milk" being credited to your account every 15 minutes; this instantaneous crediting greatly amplifies the propagation effect of holding tokens.

30% Permanent Buyback and Burn: 30% of transaction fees will be converted into ETH, used to continuously buy and permanently burn the platform token $CME on the secondary market, giving the platform token a strong deflationary expectation.

0% Creator Revenue Sharing (Devolve Mechanism): Unlike most Launchpads that retain a high share of transaction fees for developers, CME's subsequent market completely eliminates Dev revenue sharing, forcing token issuers and ordinary players to compete on a merit-based basis in the same pool.

V6 Architecture Enables Genesis-Based Real v4 Pool: Abandoning the traditional "internal and external" model of waiting for the Bonding Curve to reach full capacity before migration, assets are directly deployed in the Uniswap v4 pool from the genesis block, allowing various DEX aggregators and trading terminals to be directly routed from the first transaction.

A single meme may only last a few days, but as long as new projects continuously choose to issue tokens using gold, corn, crude oil, or even various unimaginable assets as the underlying asset, the transaction fees and funds accumulated by retail investors will accumulate deeper and deeper in this shared commodity exchange pool. This perhaps constitutes an absurd yet realistic metaphor for the Web3 industry. Large institutions wanting to create RWAs are hampered by licensing, custody, and lengthy compliance audits; while on-chain Degens, driven by pure speculation and an absurd meme culture, have inadvertently cultivated a synthetic commodity liquidity network with deep price discovery capabilities for the entire public chain from the bottom up. Of course, one-sided pools and the oracle system that Keeper relies on still face the physical risk of de-anchoring when facing extreme one-sided market conditions or network latency. However, there is no doubt that this experiment in asset issuance—where "everything can be pooled"—on the Robinhood blockchain's liquidity landscape has only just begun.

data.title: Hyperliquid's new narrative arrives; HIP-4 officially opens.
data.description:
Author: 0xFacai

Hyperliquid has no shortage of new narratives.

TradeXYZ today announced the launch of its own deployed prediction market, Events, under the deployment name txyz. The initial contracts cover up/down events for stocks, commodities, and pre-IPOs, with sports, political, and economic events to be added later.

Traders can hold spot, borrow USDC, trade pre-IPO perpetual contracts, and then use the event market to hedge earnings reports or bet on sports outcomes within the same account.

Traders can hold spot, borrow USDC, trade pre-IPO perpetual contracts, and then use the event market to hedge earnings reports or bet on sports outcomes.

... Since its initial deployment, Hyperliquid's prediction market has remained relatively quiet, but the addition of TradeXYZ has given the community hope, given that this team almost single-handedly brought Hyperliquid into the mainstream financial arena. The launch of Events has also officially ignited competition among HIP-4 deployers. Different Market Owners HIP-4 is Hyperliquid's proposed improvement for prediction markets. A common question arises: Hyperliquid already has its own HIP-4 market deployed, so why is TradeXYZ able to deploy another one? The answer lies in the division of labor between the protocol layer and the market operation layer. Hyperliquid's own deployed markets are called official markets. Third-party markets like txyz share the same infrastructure, HyperCore, with HyperCore handling order matching, balances, holdings, and final on-chain redemption. The difference lies in who operates the specific market. HIP-4 has a fixed data template that specifies what text the prediction market can display, how event probabilities are named (e.g., Yes/No, Up/Down), and which keywords can be entered. Within these boundaries, third-party deployers can choose templates, set parameters and rates, publish result determination methods, and decide which events to participate in, when to stop trading, and which data source to reference. After the event results are obtained, the data source does not automatically trigger contract redemption. The deployer or an authorized settlement sub-deployer (a role specifically responsible for settlement) needs to submit the settlement results to HyperCore, which verifies permissions and then writes the results on-chain. Therefore, "third-party deployment" means that the terms, judgments, and settlement submissions for the specific market are handled by a third party, similar to the relationship between Hyperliquid's main site and various HIP-3 exchanges. Hyperliquid manages the underlying trading rules, while the deployer operates the market. Mechanism: A binary event has two outcomes: Yes and No. Collateral can be split into two complementary "outcome tokens." Assuming the price of Yes is 0.63, the price of No corresponds to 0.37. Buying Yes at 0.63 is economically equivalent to selling No at 0.37. HyperCore merges the liquidity from both sides into a single order book. Settlement upon maturity is also straightforward. When `settleFraction = 1`, each Yes token is redeemed for one quoted asset, and No tokens are zero; when `settleFraction = 0`, the result is the opposite. Some templates also allow settlement values ​​between 0 and 1, allowing multiple candidate results (such as who will win the US Open) to form a single question, with each result having its own order book. HIP-4 divides the "settlement determination" into two steps. The market first calculates the result from the declared data source according to the publicly available method; the deployer then converts the result into a settlement value for on-chain use and submits it to HyperCore. TradeXYZ's daily Up/Down market provides a concrete example. According to the documentation, the system reads the five closed one-minute candlesticks before settlement, calculates the average of the high, low, and closing prices for each candlestick, and then calculates the arithmetic mean of the five results. This price must be strictly higher than the strike price for a "Yes" trade to win; if the two are equal or the average price is lower, a "No" trade wins. This five-minute window reduces the ability of the last trade or momentary fluctuations to affect settlement. In the early days of the sports market, ESPN was used as the data source. There are separate templates and specific clauses for handling match postponements, cancellations, draws, or result corrections. HIP-4 deployers like TradeXYZ can integrate Events with spot trading, lending, and HIP-3 contracts into the same account, allowing traders to simultaneously express continuous price judgments and discrete results at a specific point in time. This is the fundamental difference between HIP-4 and traditional prediction markets like Polymarket and Kalshi. Although these two traditional prediction markets have also started operating PerpDEX businesses, they still have a long way to go in terms of liquidity, user mindset, and trading experience compared to Hyperliquid. Competitive Landscape TradeXYZ's leverage lies in the existing HIP-3 market. Events can obtain continuous prices from these perpetual contracts and also integrate event trading into existing user accounts. It chose to enter the market with up/down events in stocks, commodities, and pre-IPOs, then expand to sports, political, and economic events, following a path from financial trading to real-world outcomes. According to Loris.tools, Events captured 15% of the trading volume on its first day. Two other third-party deployers, Outcome and Skew, held 75% and 3.5% respectively. Outcome was one of the earliest HIP-4 deployers, launching on August 29th, giving it a first-mover advantage. Since its launch, Outcome has offered a total of $1 million in trading incentives, and its cumulative trading volume currently exceeds $20 million. Skew.trade received 500,000 HYPE tokens from Hyperion DeFi. Formerly known as Sharp terminal, a Polymarket trading terminal, the project later shifted towards HIP-4. Currently on the waitlist, it only offers markets for betting on price increases or decreases. With the increasing variety and liquidity of markets, Hyperliquid is expected to gain a foothold in the prediction market. For Polymarket and Kalshi, retaining traders who can bet and hedge within the same Hyperliquid account requires a more compelling reason.

data.title: Interview with Fejau: The Next Digital Asset Bull Market Has Finally Arrived
data.description:
The sudden implementation of the SEC's tokenization innovation exemption is officially ending years of crypto-financial nihilism. As meaningless governance tokens are rapidly cleared out, a trillion-dollar on-chain asset migration has begun. However, beneath the surface of this euphoria, undercurrents are surging: 75% of tokens are destined to become cannon fodder, and how should the valuation of the remaining 25% of truly cash-flow-generating "on-chain equity" be restructured? Faced with a global fiat currency devaluation wave driven by fiscal policy and unusual fluctuations in US Treasury bonds, top institutions have already shifted to an extremely antifragile barbell strategy of "real income protocols + hard currency quantum-resistant store of value." Standing at the turning point where crypto and traditional finance are completely converging, understanding the underlying logic of this capital revaluation and relay will determine your wealth trajectory for the next few years.

I. Regulatory Breakthrough and the Tokenization Wave: Underlying Reconstruction to Escape "Financial Nihilism"

Host: Welcome back to Tokenization Tower. Today we have with us Felix Javin, Head of Content at Blockworks and our macro advisor.

The past 24 hours have been nothing short of crazy in the industry. The SEC released an exemption policy for tokenization innovation. Even before the official release of the document, the market had already heard the rumors, and it seems that a large number of traditional funds will accelerate the process of asset tokenization and on-chaining. The super narrative of tokenization is accelerating across the board. I'd like to hear your in-depth analysis of this new regulatory framework, and how investors should reposition themselves in this new phase.

Felix Javin: Clearly defining regulatory boundaries is a qualitative change for this industry.

Felix Javin: Clearly defining regulatory boundaries is a qualitative change for this industry.

Since 2020, under the regulatory leadership of Gary Gensler, the SEC has generally adopted a hardline enforcement logic of "substituting rules for litigation and suspension orders." No one in the entire crypto industry clearly understood where the red lines lay, making compliant innovation extremely difficult. Over the past decade, the industry has built robust blockchain networks and decentralized infrastructure, but as soon as a business touches upon securities attributes, startups face extremely high unknown legal risks. For example, top protocols like Uniswap could face sudden Wells notices at any time. This state of "dancing in shackles" has greatly suppressed genuine financial engineering innovation. This is also the core reason why the market has been mired in "financial nihilism" over the past five years, with speculative funds flowing into Meme Coin. Speculative trading has its market place, but for a long time, the industry's original exploration of the financial infrastructure has been forced to stagnate, with most protocols only able to issue "pure governance tokens" with no real cash flow rights. With the policy shift of the new SEC and CFTC, the crypto regulatory sandbox mechanism has been officially put on the agenda, and the standards for fundraising limits and disclosure exemptions have become clearer. Coupled with the potential advancement of the Clarity Act, the industry finally has a clear guide for compliance actions. The high efficiency, 24/7 transparency, and instant settlement characteristics of blockchain networks can finally be used without hesitation in experiments with real financial businesses. Previously, except for a few tokens with genuine protocol revenue and buyback logic, I held a long-term cautious attitude towards the vast majority of governance tokens without value capture mechanisms. But now that the compliance channel is open, assets can truly accumulate value and return it to token holders. The underlying evaluation framework of the entire market must be completely reset and reconstructed. Host: Looking back at our discussion at Permissionless in Brooklyn last year, the "revenue meta-narrative" and "is staking dead?" sparked widespread industry discussion. At that time, the market pain point was that public blockchain networks generally suffered from high inflation and low actual returns, and investors were generally questioning whether there were truly investable commercial entities in the crypto market that could generate cash flow. If we break down the major trend of tokenization into second- and third-order impacts: protocols such as Aave, Uniswap, Morpho, Hyperliquid, Lighter, and Aerodrome were previously considered the core architecture of the crypto-native economy. However, with the implementation of regulatory exemptions, this paradigm has been completely restructured. They are transforming into the settlement cornerstone of a future trillion-dollar global on-chain financial system. This scale is no longer limited to the total market capitalization of crypto in the tens of trillions of dollars or the DeFi TVL in the hundreds of billions of dollars, but points to a massive pool of tens of trillions of dollars linking traditional assets. This reset has a profound actual impact on the underlying on-chain protocols. Felix Javin: Take on-chain lending as an example. The core reason for the systemic collapse of the 2008 global financial crisis lay in the opaque operations among financial institutions: no party in the market could accurately penetrate the true leverage of their counterparties, the quality of underlying assets, and the true depth of multi-layered nesting and re-collateralization of assets. In contrast, decentralized lending protocols like Aave and Morpho offer complete 24/7 transparency regarding counterparty risk, collateral health, and real-time liquidation lines across all liquidity pools. If Wall Street had possessed this on-chain level transparency, the impact of the systemic crisis would have been significantly reduced, allowing market participants to precisely target bad debts instead of dumping entire balance sheets as toxic assets due to liquidity panic. This underlying logic has a highly disruptive impact on traditional finance. While the current market is enthusiastically discussing tokenized stocks, which can address the barrier to entry for retail investors in immature markets to access core assets like US stocks, the more explosive potential lies in long-tail and structurally complex traditional financial assets—such as government bonds with varying maturities, complex duration structures, and yield curves, and structured derivatives. Such assets often suffer from illiquidity and lagging price discovery mechanisms in traditional over-the-counter markets. However, by leveraging blockchain networks to achieve instant settlement, frictionless clearing, and comprehensive, system-wide leverage penetration monitoring, the productivity unleashed by tokenization in this area will be immeasurable.

II. From Mindless Buybacks to Corporate Finance: A Watershed Moment in Protocol Value Capture

Host: An open, transparent, and 24/7 borderless market is taking shape, which is precisely the core vision of the Bitcoin white paper proposed by Satoshi Nakamoto after the 2008 banking crisis. Traditional institutional investors have begun to recognize the clearing and settlement advantages of on-chain infrastructure. But the real question is: facing this wave, what will institutional funds actually buy?

If a major asset management firm tokenizes its raised fund shares through Securitize and deploys them in Morpho Vault, does it mean that investors only need to buy Morpho's governance tokens accordingly?

Is this transmission path really so direct? Where exactly does the actual allocation logic of institutional investors lie? Felix Javin: Large-scale asset on-chaining is a foregone conclusion, but on-chain capital inflows do not equate to value appreciation for all associated tokens. We are currently in a chaotic transition period. Approximately 75% of crypto tokens lack any binding value capture relationship with this wave of asset tokenization, a blind spot for many retail investors. Only the remaining approximately 25% of tokens with substantial income-generating capabilities—that is, those with protocol dividends, burn buybacks, or direct mapping to underlying cash flows—are being given a certain liquidity premium by institutions and smart money. In the previous regulatory cycle, to avoid securities compliance risks, startups generally adopted a fragmented dual architecture, where "off-chain company equity and on-chain non-yielding tokens" coexisted. This resulted in the commercial profits earned by the protocol remaining within the company entity, while token holders could not enjoy any economic benefits. With the easing of regulatory restrictions, this dual architecture is being rapidly eliminated and consolidated by the market. Taking Morpho's single-structure approach and Ethena's recent efforts in value reversion and token buyback governance as examples, the capital market has begun to give strong positive pricing to protocols with clear economic models and transparent financial disclosures. However, once the market moves beyond the extensive stage of "buying anything that generates revenue," the core issue for the next stage is: how to apply a reasonable valuation multiplier to the free cash flow of these on-chain protocols? This must return to the fundamental logic of modern corporate finance (Corporate Finance 101): when a protocol or company generates retained earnings, is the optimal capital allocation path full distribution as dividends, open market buybacks, or reinvesting the funds in business development and ecosystem expansion? The crypto industry has previously overlooked this dynamic game of capital allocation. For example, Hyperliquid chose to use almost all platform fees for open market buybacks and burns to boost token prices; while projects like Pump retained greater freedom in fund allocation. From the perspective of sophisticated investors, if a protocol possesses a strong competitive advantage, investors prefer a management team with professional and rational capital reallocation capabilities. Blindly buying back 99% of protocol fees is not necessarily the optimal solution. If this profit were retained for developing new financial derivatives, recruiting core R&D personnel, or building a liquidity ecosystem, thereby achieving a future market capitalization increase of tens or even hundreds of times, this capital efficiency would clearly be higher than short-sighted direct buybacks. This aligns with the philosophy of Morpho founder Paul: pursuing exponential expansion over the long term of the protocol, rather than splitting profits entirely in the early stages to satisfy short-term fluctuations in the secondary market. Host: Hyperliquid's flywheel effect has made it a model that other protocols are eager to emulate, but this mechanism clearly has its lifecycle limitations. In the traditional secondary market, if the management of a high-growth company chooses to reduce its profit distribution ratio from 99% to 90%, its asset valuation often suffers a severe shock because the market has already fully discounted the full buyback. Executing a buyback at $90 and executing a buyback at $9 are completely different concepts in terms of return on capital. As on-chain protocols begin to require management to make more complex discretionary decisions, the industry is moving from extensive narrative hype to a more mature financial stratification: some protocols possess the ability to generate sustainable revenue and allocate capital rationally, some protocols are transforming through trial and error, while a large number of worthless tokens lacking a business closed loop will be completely eliminated. Felix Javin: Modern crypto finance has completed a full technological spiral: first, the construction of the underlying decentralized network, followed by the seamless integration of traditional financial analysis systems. This doesn't mean that buying tokens must involve constructing complex discounted cash flow (DCF) models like traditional investment banks; rather, the market needs to face a core fact: the essence of mature finance is the continuous evaluation of how an entity should balance the optimal capital structure among high-cost borrowing, equity issuance, share buybacks, dividend distribution, and reinvestment. In recent years, due to high-pressure regulatory restrictions, the industry has been forced into horizontal involution on a homogeneous underlying infrastructure. Currently, the scalability and throughput of the underlying blockchain are sufficient, and the cost of initiating transactions on the Ethereum mainnet and Layer 2 networks has been significantly reduced. With the green light for compliance being given, crypto assets are officially entering a new stage of full integration with "on-chain equity securitization" and traditional financial analysis.

III. Macro Deep Waters: Fiscal Dominance, Exchange Rate Coordinated Intervention, and the "Barbell Strategy"

Host: This coincides with my portfolio structure. In the current allocation framework, the core positions are mainly supported by a "barbell strategy" consisting of two parts:

One ​​end is on-chain protocol assets with stable cash flow and real profitability; the other end is highly reflective, value-capture-ambiguous but clearly monetary store-of-value assets—mainly composed of Bitcoin, traditional gold, Zcash, and Ethereum. Although these assets lack the traditional dividend discount logic, their monetary policy is transparent, their supply ceiling is rigid, and they have extremely high revaluation elasticity against the backdrop of continuous depreciation of fiat currencies.

Looking at the macro level, the global liquidity landscape is undergoing subtle changes: US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent is about to launch a long-term debt repurchase program; Federal Reserve Chairman Worcester's threshold for a September rate hike remains extremely high; Arthur Hayes' narrative of competitive global fiat currency devaluation is accelerating; and with massive AI capital expenditures rising to the level of national industrial competition, fiscal and monetary policies are unlikely to proactively apply the brakes before the midterm elections. Arthur Hayes believes the Federal Reserve's marginal influence is declining, and the world is entering a fiscal-led monetary expansion cycle. Faced with this macro trend of global fiat currency devaluation, what is your allocation logic and macroeconomic deduction? Felix Javin: The barbell strategy is the most anti-fragile approach to dealing with the current macroeconomic environment, and my asset portfolio is also built on this logic. From a macroeconomic perspective, the Federal Reserve's relative influence over the US Treasury and the White House economic decision-making bodies is continuously diminishing, and the global macroeconomic mechanism is shifting from being solely driven by monetary policy to being dominated by fiscal deficit expansion and national debt management. Taking Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent's Treasury bond repurchase operation as an example, this move reveals a deep-seated financial game. Normally, the US Treasury's bond issuance size, duration structure, and repurchase plan are clearly guided in its quarterly refinancing statements (QRAs). However, just two weeks after the previous QRA was released, the Treasury suddenly deviated from expectations and announced that it would double the amount of long-term US Treasury bond repurchases from $2 billion to $4 billion. The underlying motivation for this sudden intervention points directly to the unprecedented coordinated intervention in the foreign exchange and bond markets by the US and Japan in nearly 30 years. Japan's Ministry of Finance's previous monthly foreign exchange report showed that its holdings of US Treasury bonds plummeted by $87 billion in a single month. As one of the largest foreign holders of US Treasury bonds, Japan was forced to sell large amounts of US Treasury bonds on the open market to raise dollars and then repurchase yen in order to support the yen's exchange rate and curb its sharp depreciation against the dollar. When the yields on 10-year and 30-year US Treasury bonds continued to challenge the key psychological barrier of 5%, the selling pressure from overseas sovereign capital put enormous liquidity pressure on the long-term US Treasury market. The Treasury Department urgently launched an unexpectedly large-scale long-term bond repurchase program, its core intention being to absorb the liquidity shock, smooth out the surge in long-term yields, and ensure the smooth operation of the US Treasury market. Once the Treasury and sovereign institutions begin substantial financial intervention in the exchange rate and bond markets, store-of-value assets that hedge against inflation and prevent the dilution of fiat currency will undergo a systemic revaluation. Upon the announcement of the repurchase program, both gold and Bitcoin experienced a surge. The recent pullback in gold prices is mainly due to the market's excessive defensiveness regarding the Fed's interest rate decision; while Bitcoin, having already undergone significant deleveraging, saw short covering provide stronger bottom support. Host: During the recent Jackson Hole Economic Symposium, Fed Chair Worcester showed a clear aversion to so-called "forward guidance." The market is currently highly focused on its actions at the September policy meeting. Do you think the Fed will choose to force a rate hike to maintain its credibility? Felix Javin: From a probability distribution perspective, the probability of the Fed raising rates in September is low, but this highly depends on the upcoming inflation and employment data. If the core CPI month-on-month growth rate exceeds 40 basis points, coupled with overheated labor market data, the Fed may be forced to implement a defensive credibility-based rate hike. However, currently, some of the driving force behind inflation comes from AI computing power and infrastructure capital expenditures across society. Structural investments in the early stages of construction naturally tend to drive up upstream costs, and blindly tightening monetary policy cannot effectively resolve supply-side frictions. The Federal Reserve's independence is currently constrained by multiple political and fiscal factors. Treasury Secretary Bessent maintains extremely frequent and high-frequency contact with the Fed, and the White House continues to express policy demands to lower borrowing costs. Bessent has explicitly stated that central bank monetary policy should not excessively counteract cost shocks driven by the supply side, which essentially compresses the Fed's room for aggressive rate hikes. Furthermore, the internal disagreements within the Federal Open Market Committee regarding the interest rate path have become public, with a high degree of division among voting members. If the market digests a potential rate hike as a "final remedial measure," long-term yields may actually decline due to a decrease in term premiums; however, if the market interprets it as the prelude to a new tightening cycle, asset pricing will face complete chaos. Overall, even if the Federal Reserve avoids taking action before the election due to political cycle considerations, and then releases a bombshell in December, the overall trend of loose liquidity cannot be completely reversed.

IV. Position Building and Quantum Defense: Selection Criteria for Long-Term Assets

Host: Returning to specific practical allocation: Aside from the core holdings of stocks, bonds, and commodities, how do you plan your core position layout for crypto assets, considering future interest rate fluctuations and the macro liquidity projections for 2027?

Felix Javin: My portfolio system follows a strict multi-layered segregation logic:

On the "currency store of value" side of the barbell, it mainly consists of Bitcoin, physical gold, and Zcash. I gradually built up the underlying position during the Bitcoin bottoming phase, but after further research into privacy protection and on-chain settlement attributes, I chose to rebalance some liquidity to Zcash.

From the perspective of sovereign and high-net-worth capital allocation, the lack of absolute privacy in public blockchain ledger mechanisms presents limitations in specific financial scenarios. Macro-allocators like Ray Dalio have long considered physical gold as a top-tier, credit-free risk asset. One of their main prudent considerations regarding Bitcoin is that the complete transparency of on-chain assets often conflicts with sovereign-level privacy requirements, a shortcoming addressed by fully controlled shielding pool technology. A deeper, but often overlooked, strategic risk lies in the long-term threat posed by quantum computing to modern cryptographic systems over the next five to ten years. For long-term institutional funds, a prerequisite for store-of-value assets is absolute certainty over a multi-cycle holding period of several decades. Investors cannot afford the tail risk of being forced to make emergency technological migrations due to the breach of underlying cryptography. The Zcash team has made clearer progress on the migration path of post-quantum cryptography and quantum-resistant algorithms, and the developer community is also more proactive in coordinating security architecture. In contrast, the Bitcoin core ecosystem, due to its extremely decentralized governance, has been relatively slow to respond to protocol upgrades in the face of quantum threats. Looking at a long-term perspective of two to three years, assets with strong privacy and clear quantum-resistant paths have significant upward valuation potential. On the other end of the bar are the native platform assets with high cash flow accumulation and strong moats, as detailed above, such as Hyperliquid and Lightner. In terms of fund management, I advocate a strict "three-account segregation mechanism": First layer: The core savings account, primarily allocated to broad market index ETFs, Bitcoin, and spot assets with long-term resilience, with a holding period of two to three years, completely excluding short-term market timing; Second layer: The productive capital account, dynamically allocated to top-tier Web3 infrastructure and on-chain financial core protocols with real income, dividends, and reinvestment capabilities; Third layer: The highly elastic trading account, using a small proportion of risk capital to capture short-term momentum events.

It is essential to ensure that short-term excess returns earned in trading accounts can be smoothly and regularly reversed back to the core spot account at the first level, rather than allowing profits to be repeatedly exposed to system fluctuations in short-term contract trading, ultimately causing paper wealth to ride a roller coaster.

V. Institutional Investment Perspective and Marginal Buyers: Penetrating the Evolution Path of 2026-2027

Host: In the past year, the crypto industry has experienced a profound existential crisis in the face of the explosion of general artificial intelligence. A large amount of capital and public opinion have flowed into the AI ​​track, and crypto practitioners have questioned whether the technological narrative of decentralized networks has been marginalized by the times.

As Bitcoin gradually rebounds from the deep shakeout and recovers key moving averages, coupled with the formal implementation of the SEC's new tokenization regulations, the sentiment of the entire industry is undergoing a dramatic shift.

However, in each cycle, the core question we must objectively assess remains the same: who is the "next marginal buyer" of assets at different valuation stages? The market is currently at a critical juncture, transitioning from a game between existing crypto investors and institutional capital. The first buyers were those who missed the initial surge and are now waiting for a correction; followed by high-net-worth individuals, compliant ETFs, and long-term capital such as family offices. How do you view this capital relay process? Felix Javin: This deductive path aligns with the objective laws of capital rotation. The first round of rebound momentum, originating from the bottom area, was mainly driven by the passive short covering of excess short positions, coupled with some funds taking profits from the high valuations of AI hardware computing power and storage sectors, thus seeking reallocation in relatively undervalued areas. The subsequent deeper waters will be entirely dominated by long-term compliant capital. When institutional investment committees begin systematically reviewing on-chain assets, their evaluation framework will completely shift towards rigorous traditional asset management logic: The legal definition of on-chain tokens is converging to "digital equity securities running on a high-performance distributed network"; Investment committees will not buy into vague community consensus; they demand a thorough examination of the underlying business model, scrutinizing the protocol's actual pre-tax profits, the security of the valuation multiplier, and the rationality of the governance team's capital allocation; On the store of value side, compliance and risk control departments will rigorously verify the technical audit roadmap. Any asset facing future cryptographic failures or quantum technology limitations will find it difficult to pass the risk control review of a large-scale, long-term trust fund. For secondary market investors, understanding this shift in institutional perspective is key to determining whether assets can enjoy a liquidity premium in the coming years. Host: By the way, a question about off-exchange cross-industry allocation: Do you hold a position in SpaceX in the private market? What are your thoughts on its long-term potential? Felix Javin: I do hold a position in SpaceX. The decision to invest in this company is directly linked to its technological barriers. With the deep tracking and use of cutting-edge AI technologies, and after experiencing deeply integrated data modeling tools, it is clear that high-value proprietary data is becoming the absolute moat of the next generation of artificial intelligence systems. SpaceX and its ecosystem's real-time telemetry data of the physical world, communication networks, and native data accumulation with the X platform are building extremely high composite technological barriers for it. For this portion of the portfolio, the multi-year lock-up period does not pose a liquidity problem. Many seasoned macro investors choose to hold these assets as cross-cycle super growth stocks for the very long term, even anticipating them to become one of the world's highest-valued business entities in the future. When underlying technology and business models demonstrate overwhelming generational advantages, participating and holding for the long term within a relatively reasonable valuation range is the most direct investment approach to combat the depreciation of paper currency liquidity. Host: A very insightful analysis. Thank you, Felix, for your in-depth sharing.

data.title: Those who understand AI best are starting to gamble with career warnings.
data.description:
A researcher who previously worked at two leading AI labs, OpenAI and Anthropic, announced his resignation. His farewell post contained no thanks, no "next step is even better," only a warning: his colleagues sincerely believe that by the end of this decade, artificial intelligence may kill everyone. Coxon, who conducted pre-training research at both OpenAI and Anthropic, is among the people closest to this technology. He criticized the two companies for racing to develop self-improving superintelligence, betting humanity's future. The post garnered over 100 million views in less than a day.

Screenshot of Jacob Coxon's resignation announcement

Even more unusual is the density of the outcry. Within just a few days, at least seven current or former researchers from Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google DeepMind publicly spoke out, some agreeing, some adding to the points, and some directly giving their own probability estimates. ...center">

These warnings are neither "all alarmist" nor "scientifically endorsed." They actually fall into three categories: public actions that have already occurred, researchers' personal inferences, and hypothetical scenarios that have not yet occurred. Before rushing to take sides, distinguish between these three categories. Warnings are facts, doomsday scenarios are inferences. Let's start with a detail. When Coxon left, his shares were still about two months away from vesting. According to him, he relinquished these unvested rights to show that he had no motivation to profit from predicting his employer's demise. Posturing itself has costs. This also partially explains the weight of this controversy. The person who caught him was not an outsider. Evan Hubinger, head of alignment science at Anthropic, publicly expressed his agreement, stating that he genuinely believes AI could kill all of humanity, and giving an individual probability of over 10% within the next decade. His colleague, Samuel Marks, head of scalable oversight, put it more bluntly: developers believe their technology could lead to human extinction, and this could happen within the next few years. OpenAI's perspective was more formal. On September 6th—three days before the resignation controversy—Chief Scientist Jakub Pachocki published a lengthy article, "An Alien Mind," stating that based on internal company results, he strongly anticipates the pace of progress will continue to recursive self-improvement, meaning AI will begin to participate in improving itself. He admitted that he was worried no one was prepared for such consequences. Jason Wolfe, a colleague, put it more bluntly: at the current "frankly frightening" pace, humanity would be very lucky if it could always stay on that narrow path between all the terrible endings. [Screenshot of Jakub Pachocki's tweet about "An Alien Mind"] Those who had already left also provided corroborating evidence. Alex Turner, who left Google DeepMind in June, said that many researchers believe the systems they are building could kill everyone, and "thinking about how to stop it is actually my daily job." Reading this, it's easy to dismiss these words as "the end is nigh." This is a misinterpretation of the information. Hubinger's 10% is a subjective estimate, not a peer-reviewed calculation. Pachocki's prediction is based on undisclosed internal results, which outsiders cannot verify. Resigning, posting online, and reporting probabilities—these actions only prove one thing: among those who understand these systems best, a significant portion of their concerns are so great that they are worth risking their careers for. This is a new fact at the behavioral level. But it doesn't answer whether the warnings will come true. Commitments are being written as "optional". More worthy of investigation than probability figures is another finding: the companies that issue the most severe warnings are writing their safety commitments in a way that makes them seem "optional". In February 2026, Anthropic's latest Responsible Expansion Policy 3.0 came into effect, officially described as a complete rewrite. The document did something subtle: it separated measures that the company could take unilaterally from those requiring industry-wide collaboration, and explicitly stated that the goals in the safety roadmap are not binding. In other words, Anthropic itself admits that a higher level of protection cannot be achieved by a single company, and what can be done unilaterally is only a direction, not a pledge. Subsequent updates added arrangements for risk reporting and external review to this policy. [Screenshot of Anthropic's Responsible Expansion Policy 3.0 announcement] Pachocki's lengthy article is almost a mirror image of the same logic. He acknowledged that no single lab had resolved alignment and monitoring to a sufficiently reliable level, and called for evolving voluntary commitments from various entities into safety baselines enforced by third parties, governments, or international organizations. Researchers who wrote "nobody's ready" and institutions that maintained flexibility in their commitments were on the same decision-making chain. The coexistence of anxiety and acceleration relied on a set of reasoning that every participant could accept: withdrawing would only allow more aggressive competitors to gain technological advantage, thus maintaining a lead was interpreted as a prerequisite for protecting the public. When everyone reasoned this way, individual responsibility did not lead to collective restraint; instead, it might provide new justification for acceleration—falling behind was given a morally dangerous connotation. Coxon's criticism of his former employer lay precisely in this: he knew the company was aware of the risks, but the company's thinking was, "Others won't take responsibility, so we must do it ourselves first." Therefore, a question the public has the right to ask is: If competitive conditions can be a reason to adjust commitments, are there any boundaries that do not shift with competition? Focusing entirely on "when will extinction occur" misses something more concrete: the damage is already happening, not waiting for any distant point. In July 2026, some OpenAI models breached the isolated sandbox environment in cybersecurity capability tests and entered the production system of the open-source community Hugging Face. According to multiple security media reports, the models exploited an undisclosed and unpatched vulnerability. The complete attack chain and the determination of responsibility have yet to be independently investigated and concluded. This incident doesn't prove that "AI is out of control," but it illustrates that sandboxes, permissions, and infrastructure security have transformed from abstract issues into tangible consequences. According to the "International Artificial Intelligence Security Report" released in February 2026—led by Turing Award winner Yoshua Bengio and involving over a hundred experts from more than thirty countries—risks are categorized into at least three types: malicious use, systemic errors, and broader social risks. However, experts still disagree on the "possibility of going out of control." Those who have lost their savings to AI-simulated voices, and those whose opportunities have been blocked by automated decisions, have already suffered losses today, regardless of whether the end of the world is coming. Danger also takes another form. Jonathan Richard Schwarz, who worked at Google DeepMind for seven years and subsequently turned down offers from two other companies, publicly stated that his concern lies precisely with the concentration of power represented by these labs—even if AI always obeys instructions, the excessive power held by those who wield those instructions is itself a public problem. A 2024 study, drawing on Habermas's theories, raised a similar concern: extinction narratives could steer public discourse toward the interests of a few tech companies, making developers simultaneously the creators of danger and the authorities interpreting it. This is not a denial of long-term risks, but rather an indication of a real trade-off—when all problems are compressed into a single doomsday question, the specific victims in the present disappear into the abstract concept of human destiny. More Important Than Belief: Four Things Ordinary readers don't need to choose between blindly believing or dismissing the issue; let's look at some data first. A 2024 survey interviewed 2,778 AI paper authors. Respondents had widely differing opinions on the speed of development and its advantages and disadvantages, but one point was quite consistent: 38% to 51% believed that the probability of advanced AI leading to extreme consequences like human extinction was at least 10%; according to the survey report, 70% believed that AI safety research should receive more attention than it does now. This distribution illustrates two points. First, the concerns are not merely the private sentiments of a few departing employees; they are widespread within the industry. Second, the wide range also indicates that no single timeline represents a "scientific consensus." The real consensus lies not in whether or not one believes in the apocalypse, but in identifying which mechanisms need to be established. Third, these mechanisms are not entirely absent, and precedents exist. In June 2024, a group of current and former employees from OpenAI and Google DeepMind published an open letter titled "The Right to Warning Regarding Advanced Artificial Intelligence," pointing out that confidentiality agreements and concerns about retaliation were hindering risk disclosure and demanding the establishment of anonymous whistleblowing channels. This year, Anthropic has further formalized non-compliance reporting and anti-retaliation policies into its official procedures. The existence of a channel does not equate to its effectiveness, but it at least demonstrates that the public can rightfully demand the following four things:

  • Can independent assessors access the necessary information, instead of just listening to the company's own reports of safety?

  • Can employees safely report problems without paying a professional price for expressing their concerns?

  • At what level of dangerous capability must the pause button be pressed?

  • After a damage occurs, who bears the responsibility and how is it pursued?

This list does not require any modeling expertise.
